pr_title: Adds support for extending algo time loop for long-running scheduled events
pr_body:
#### Description
Adds support for long-running scheduled events. When a scheduled event is detected to have exceed one full second of execution time, we'll start requesting 'minutes' from a leaky bucket implementation managed by the `AlgorithmManager` via a proxy that also controls the delegate provided to the `Isolator`. When a scheduled event calls `AlgorithmTimeLimitManager.RequestAdditionalTime(int minutes)`, it increases the maximum amount of time the algorithm is allowed to spend in a single time loop.


 We restrict each algorithm time loop to a pre-determined amount of time.
Exceeding this limit will cause the algorithm to immediately terminate.
This quickly becomes an issue when considering users running trainable
models that have a long initialization period that exceeds the time loop
maximum.

This change provides a mechanism through which a long-running scheduled
event is permitted to keep running and is permitted to avoid the time loop
permitted by requesting additional time. Requests for additional time are
limited according to a leaky bucket implementation whose parameters are
set via the job's controls structure. The fundamental time unit for the
algorithm is a single minute.

Here's how it works. If a scheduled event takes longer than one full wall
clock second then a request is made to the leaky bucket for one more minute.
If the scheduled event continues to take more time, it will continue to
request additional minutes. Each requested minute will prevent the algorithm's
time loop check from terminating the algorithm. When the bucket is empty and
no more minutes are available to be requested, a TimeoutException is thrown
causing a cascade that ends in the algorithm's termination and status being
flipped to RuntimeError.

Additionally, this applies equally to ALL scheduled events. While some helpers
were added with the naming of Train and TrainNow to the ScheduleManager, these
methods don't do anything special and the infrastructure doesn't otherwise
flag them as different, so this feature becomes part of the core Scheduled
Event feature set.

Further, the live scheduled events were not touched and are still pending
further discussion regarding the value added by enforcing a time restriction
when simulation time and wall clock time are equivalent.

#### Related Issue

#### Motivation and Context
<!--- Why is this change required? What problem does it solve? -->
The aim of this change is to provide a controlled mechanism for users to run ML training that can potentially take a fairly large amount of time (up to 2 hours) without running afoul of the algorithm manager's time loop limit restrictions. We also seek to limit the total amount of time an algorithm can do this through a leaky bucket implementation whose parameters are set via the job packet.

#### Requires Documentation Change
<!--- Please indicate if these changes will require updates to documentation, and if so, specify what changes are required -->
Yes. We should add the new training methods to the API documentation along with a description of behavior and the default time limits.

Unit tests added for new components and additional tests added to check certain aspects of the integrated implementation. Also, two regression tests are added to validate throwing and refill behavior when running full stack.

issue_context.title: Custom Timeouts for Training Models
issue_context.body:
With the rise of AI it is becoming more common to do expensive computations in a strategy which might take a while. LEAN currently has a limit of 10 minutes per loop of the algorithm designed to prevent an algorithm locking up and crashing without user awareness.

We need a way to train these models for longer periods.

#### Expected Behavior
Some mechanism for training models -- with a maximum timeout controlled by the Controls class. 

#### Actual Behavior
No safe way to do computations longer than 10min. 

#### Potential Solution
Helper method:
QCA.Train( action, defaultTimeout = 30min, callback=null, synchronous=true)

or "semaphore" flag for 1x increases in the timeout:
QCA.LoopTimeout = TimeSpan.FromMinutes(30);

#### Reproducing the Problem
Run any backtest with long processing intra-loop. 

#### Checklist 
- [x] I have completely filled out this template
- [x] I have confirmed that this issue exists on the current `master` branch
- [x] I have confirmed that this is not a duplicate issue by searching [issues](https://github.com/QuantConnect/Lean/issues)

It would be good to have a global setting, with a default of 5 minutes, that can be overwritten in the `Initialize` function.

review_comments: Nice 👍
It seems we wait 1 minute till we request more time for the first time 🤔, seems this might cause some unexpected behavior

My reasoning is I didn't want to charge users a _full_ minute just because their scheduled event took more than ~2ms or so (however long it takes to spin up the task and pass the `finished` check). Eventually those minutes would drain. Another important thing to note here is that time has been quantized at the minute, as opposed to tracking ticks (time spans).
Right, and since we are covered by the initial 10 min window there shouldn't be any issues 👍
We are not setting `_failed` here?

This is a `TryXXX` pattern. By convention, `TryXXX` methods don't throw exceptions and shouldn't corrupt the state of the object. If the consumer wants an error thrown if additional time can't be requested, then they need to call the `RequestAdditionalTime(int)` method.
If this class is only used in tests it might make sense to move it there

It's actually part of the ported code from the referenced github repository. That being said, I think it rounds out the `ISleepStrategy` space and to be honest, I _really_ like the idea of an `ISleepStrategy`. Think about all the hard coded `Thread.Sleep( _n_ )` everywhere. I'm happy to move it to tests if there are strong opinions here, but in my opinion, it doesn't negatively impact anything and  rounds out the `ISleepStrategy` concept by showing some possible other implementations.
Might be a good idea for these algorithms (Py/C#) to assert that the training was executed, eg set a flag and check it `OnEndOfAlgorithm` and throw if they didn't run

This regression algorithm aims to verify that the leaky bucket is emptied, as mentioned in the comment. I think adding a flag obscures the point of this test and would be just another test of the well established scheduled events feature.

I'm _really_ glad you brought this one up though, it made me double check `RegressionTests.cs` and noticed that I had changed the name of this test (used to be `TrainingOnDataRegressionAlgorithm`). So I've updated the regression test to reference the correct algorithm name. 👍

I think it would be important to reduce the execution time of these new algorithms (Py/C#) so they don't add such a big overhead to the suite, we should be able to test the feature with seconds? - Note that today **155** algos take ~3 minutes to run

3 minutes? The regression test suit takes 30+ on my machine... hmm...  It technically needs at least two full minutes since the leaky bucket quantizes time by the minute. So even if the algorithm time loop limit is set to one tick, we'll still wait a minute before deducting time from the leaky bucket and then another full minute before we check again and it fails. The goal of this test is to have it pull one from the bucket and the next one fail.

What we can do is simply disable these from running, either by setting `CanRunLocally = false` or by removing the `IRegressionAlgorithmDefinition` implementation.

`takes 30+ on my machine` that's a lot! 😮 - `Note that today 155 algos take ~3 minutes to run` I wasn't counting the entire test suite but just the regression algorithms, I think setting `CanRunLocally = false` make sense

Consumers might not know the capacity, maybe it's worth adding it to the exception, eg requested 'X' capacity is 'Y'

These exceptions will go up: `LeakyBucket.TryConsume()` -> `AlgorithmTimeLimitManager.TryRequestAdditionalTime()` -> `AlgorithmTimeLimitManager.RequestAdditionalTime()`-> `IsolatorLimitResultProvider.Consume()` and kill the monitoring task? but no one will know of it? 🤔

True, but an exception like that would typically arise from a misconfigured system. That being said, I agree that a consumer should be able to determine the limits of valid inputs without knowing how the type was constructed. I'll add `ITokenBucket.Capacity` so the abstraction is self contained. Great comment! 👍
RE: specific stack and potential for error: luckily we're using a literal `1` for the `minutes` parameters (which becomes `tokens`).
Not sure whats the use case for this `Consume` implementation, it will block the calling thread until the time tokens are available
Leaky bucket is a rate limiting algorithm. So this `Consume` method is _arguably_ the reason the entire class exists.
If we are not going to be using the blocking `Consume` implementation I'm not sure I see the value on these implementations/interfaces, I'd be more inclined to simplify if possible

In general, I think it's _very_ beneficial to design concepts and solutions in isolation from the current task. My general design philosophy works by first identifying the problem(s) that need to be solved. In this case, my design called for a leaky bucket implementation, so the first major commit in this PR is indeed, a full featured leaky bucket algorithm. After designing the component _at the core_ of this entire PR, I then proceeded to implement the specifics of the problem at hand.

Over the years I've learned that there is certainly balance between _just enough_ and *way* too much. In the case of these implementations, they're ported from the referenced github library, so they don't cost us anything, but provide solid abstractions and implementations to act as fundamental building blocks for future solutions. While I don't think everything should be componentized, I do find that development continues to get easier and easier if you follow this kind of approach due to the quality of the building blocks available to you.
Wondering which is the `referenced github library`?

I left a note in the source [here](https://github.com/QuantConnect/Lean/pull/3743/files#diff-dc9ad5005cc9b09a90ed99a877a77eb2R26). It's based on this [`TokenBucket`](https://github.com/mxplusb/TokenBucket) dotnet core repository.
Isn't the caller already checking this?

There's more than one caller and in `BacktestingRealTimeResultHandler` there's two difference guard clauses around the invocation. They actually have different intent as well. Also, in general I prefer to not make decisions in a method based on it's consumers. Now, the inverse isn't true -- so if there's a change that _should_ be made here (I'm not saying there is), then I would want to change the consumer of this function and not this function. The purposes of this guard clause is to prevent spinning up the task in the function in invokes just so the scheduled event can say 'its not time yet'.
Docs seems to need an update after the last commit
Not sure how will `RealTimeProvider.Instance` work for backtesting, shouldn't it be related to the algorithms Time instead?
In this case, the resources we're rate limiting is CPU time itself, hence using the real time provider.
Should it be `tokens >= _available`, can we consume all available? Maybe this log would be better as an error log

We can consume all of the tokens but this condition is checking the opposite. It's asking if there's not enough tokens (requested more than available). I don't view this as an error condition since it's in a `TryXXX` method and the consumer has enough information at its disposal to perform the same logging, if desired.
Good idea 😄

yea, I know, I'm kind of anal about it 😛 

I just spend _soooo_ much time reading code, I normally don't notice doing it anymore until I'm doing my self review lol
We might want to request time _before_ the minute/time we have is over, to avoid any race conditions with the monitoring thread

It sounds like you're referring to potential [nyquist] effects. I'm not sure which monitoring thread you're referring to as there's only a single thread checking times here. The maximum error in this check is based on the sleep interval of this loop, which is currently set to 5ms. So every 5ms we check if a full minute has passed, and if so, we request an extra minute. 

After writing the above, I think there's some misunderstanding here. As soon as the monitoring task starts (_very_ close to when the scheduled event starts), we start checking how long it's been running, every 5ms. When it's been running for a minimum of 1 full minute, we go and request an additional minute. The desired behavior here being that the first minute was free, but the _next_ one, you'll have to pay for. If there are minutes available in the bucket, then we increment to check the following minute, and so on and so forth. When the bucket runs out of minutes _and then_ you request another minute, the `_failed` flag will be flipped and the isolator will terminate the algorithm.
Idem question about whats the use case for this implementation
This provides a `TimeSpan` overload, merely for convenience.
